title: Data Centres Energy Demand Outlook in Australia
gist: Oxford Economics Australia and AEMO jointly forecast Australian data centre electricity consumption rising from 5.1 TWh in FY26 to 15.5 TWh by FY30 and 33.7 TWh by FY36 in the NEM under the central Step Change scenario — a 31%/47% upgrade on the 2025 vintage driven by a much larger connection-request pipeline. Demand stays >85% concentrated in NSW and Victoria, where data centres would take ~12% of state grid-supplied electricity by FY30 and 19% by FY36, and the modelling now explicitly discounts 'phantom demand' with probabilistic project weighting.

insights.claim: Australian data centre electricity consumption in the National Electricity Market is forecast to roughly triple from 5.1 TWh in FY26 to 15.5 TWh by FY30, then more than double again to 33.7 TWh by FY36 under the central Step Change scenario (5.2, 15.8 and 34.3 TWh respectively on a national basis).
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: A ~6.6x rise in a decade sets the demand baseline for Australian generation, transmission and gen-tailer earnings — size new supply build against this curve, not historic load growth.
insights.quote: data centre electricity consumption across the NEM is forecast to increase from 5.1 TWh in FY26 (5.2 TWh nationally) to 15.5 TWh (15.8 TWh nationally) by FY30 and 33.7 TWh (34.3 TWh nationally) by FY36
insights.locator: Headline research findings

insights.claim: Near-term Australian data centre load growth comes almost entirely from ramping and expanding existing sites rather than greenfield builds, because connected and committed capacity is still moving toward mature operating levels.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: Pre-FY30 demand is high-confidence and largely locked in — the load is coming whether or not the new-build pipeline converts, which favours near-term firming and grid-connection plays.
insights.quote: The near-term outlook is primarily driven by the ramp-up of existing data centres and likely expansions of existing sites.
insights.locator: The near-term outlook is primarily driven

insights.claim: After FY30 the growth driver flips to entirely new data centres moving through the project pipeline, and forecast uncertainty rises materially from that point because of planning, commercial and delivery hurdles.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: Treat FY30 as the regime break: anything underwritten on post-FY30 data centre load carries pipeline-conversion risk, not just demand risk.
insights.quote: Due to the inherent uncertainty of how many of these projects progress through planning, commercial and delivery hurdles, uncertainty in the forecasts increases materially from FY30.
insights.locator: After FY30, new data centres become the main driver

insights.claim: Even in AEMO's Slower Growth scenario Australian data centre demand keeps compounding — to 10.5 TWh by FY30 and 15.1 TWh by FY36 in the NEM — because existing facilities, likely expansions and well-progressed prospective projects continue ramping without needing large-scale new development.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: The downside case still triples FY26 load by FY36 — the asymmetry favours being long Australian electricity demand; the bear case is slower growth, not decline.
insights.quote: Data centre demand continues to grow even under Slower Growth, reaching 10.5 TWh (10.8 TWh nationally) by FY30 and 15.1 TWh (15.7 TWh nationally) by FY36
insights.locator: Data centre demand continues to grow even under

insights.claim: AEMO's Accelerated Transition scenario — faster cloud adoption, stronger AI demand, more international workloads and higher pipeline conversion — lifts NEM data centre demand to 20.1 TWh by FY30 and 52.5 TWh by FY36, with Victoria and transmission-connected developments taking a larger share.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: The bull-to-bear FY36 spread is 15.1 to 52.5 TWh — a 3.5x fan that is itself the trade: optionality on Australian generation and transmission is underpriced relative to the central case.
insights.locator: Accelerated Transition reflects a stronger development cycle

insights.claim: New South Wales and Victoria account for over 85% of NEM data centre electricity consumption all the way out to FY36, making Australian data centre load a two-state grid story rather than a national one.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: Localise the exposure: NSW and VIC transmission, connection queues and firming capacity are where the demand shock lands, not Queensland or South Australia.
insights.quote: Demand remains concentrated in New South Wales and Victoria, with the two regions accounting for over 85% of NEM data centre electricity consumption to FY36.
insights.locator: Demand remains concentrated in New South Wales

insights.claim: Data centres are forecast to consume around 12% of total state grid-supplied electricity in NSW and Victoria by FY30, rising to 19% by FY36 — meaning roughly one in five units of state grid electricity serves data centres within a decade.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: A single customer class at ~19% of state load reshapes network planning, tariff politics and retail competition — watch for regulatory intervention on connection priority and cost allocation.
insights.quote: Data centres are forecast to consume around 12% of total state grid-supplied electricity in NSW and VIC by FY30, rising to 19% by FY36.
insights.locator: The concentration of data centres in New South Wales

insights.claim: The upside scenario shifts the geographic and connection mix toward Victoria and transmission-connected (rather than distribution-connected) developments, implying the largest hyperscale campuses land on high-voltage infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: Transmission-connected growth favours network owners and large-scale generation PPAs over distribution-level solutions — a signal for where capex flows if AI demand surprises to the upside.
insights.locator: Accelerated Transition reflects a stronger development cycle

insights.claim: The 2026 Step Change forecast is a material upgrade on the 2025 vintage: energy demand is 31% higher by FY30, 47% higher by FY36, then moderates to a 27% upgrade by FY50.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: Consecutive large upward revisions are the tell — official demand forecasts have been chasing the AI build-out, so the current central case may still under-shoot.
insights.quote: Under Step Change, energy demand is 31% higher by FY30 and 47% by FY36, before moderating to 27% in the long run by FY50.
insights.locator: The 2026 forecasts are a material upgrade from 2025

insights.claim: The upgrade is driven by connection requests that are significantly higher than in 2025 in MW terms, plus updated core assumptions from recent data releases — i.e. the revision is grounded in observed developer behaviour rather than model recalibration alone.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: Connection-request MW is the leading indicator to track between forecast vintages — it moved first and dragged the official numbers with it.
insights.quote: The upgrade reflects the larger development pipeline, with connection requests significantly higher than in 2025 in MW terms alongside updated core assumptions informed by recent data releases.
insights.locator: The 2026 forecasts are a material upgrade from 2025

insights.claim: The FY36 upgrade (47%) exceeds the FY30 upgrade (31%) while the FY50 upgrade moderates to 27%, implying the revision is concentrated in the mid-2030s pipeline rather than a permanent level shift in structural demand.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: The modellers expect saturation, not perpetual compounding — long-dated generation assets underwritten on extrapolated AI load growth face a flattening terminal curve.
insights.locator: The 2026 forecasts are a material upgrade from 2025

themes.theme: Phantom demand and probabilistic pipeline modelling

insights.claim: The 2026 model now assigns each prospective data centre project a statistically determined probability of progression instead of a binary likely/unlikely call, explicitly to strip out 'phantom demand' from withdrawn or duplicated projects.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: A reusable discipline for any AI-infrastructure pipeline: headline announced capacity overstates real load, so probability-weight the queue before sizing supply.
insights.quote: This provides a more structured way to account for potential phantom demand while integrating information from current market activity to inform the outlook.
insights.locator: Probabilistic weighting was introduced in the Project Approach

insights.claim: Announced data centre projects are systematically inflated because multiple developers lodge separate connection requests responding to the same underlying demand, and some projects are filed before commercial, planning and connection hurdles are resolved.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: Double-counting in connection queues means gross announced MW is a bad proxy for real capacity — discount headline pipeline figures in any market, not just Australia.
insights.quote: Some projects may be withdrawn, duplicated across multiple developers responding to the same underlying demand, or lodged before commercial, planning and connection hurdles have been resolved.
insights.locator: Probabilistic weighting was introduced in the Project Approach

insights.claim: Progression probabilities are derived from observed year-on-year changes in the connection request database between 2025 and 2026, using project status, connection status, localised competition and whether the proposed timeline is realistic.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: Localised competition as a discount factor implies clustered projects in the same node cannibalise each other's odds — a screening rule for assessing individual site announcements.
insights.locator: These probabilities are statistically determined by observed changes

insights.claim: The probabilistic weighting rests on only a single year of connection-database history and will only become robust as more years accumulate, so the current discount on prospective projects is itself weakly evidenced.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: The methodology's key innovation is the least-tested part of the model — treat the post-FY30 numbers as scenario-grade, not forecast-grade.
insights.quote: The probabilistic project weighting will become more robust as additional years of data are collected, providing a larger sample size for analysis.
insights.locator: We expect to continue refining the model methodology

themes.theme: Electricity intensity and AI compositional shift

insights.claim: Electricity consumption per dollar spent on web and data services is now modelled as a logistic curve rather than a linear trend, because recent data shows faster short-term intensity growth that settles as the market matures.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: S-curve intensity means the steepest energy-per-dollar growth is happening now — front-load the demand shock and expect the ratio to plateau rather than compound indefinitely.
insights.locator: A logistic curve has been adopted to forecast the intensity

insights.claim: The intensity acceleration is attributed to a compositional shift within digital services — from traditional web and data services toward more electricity-intensive cloud, AI and data processing activity — rather than to growth in digital spending itself.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: Energy demand can surge even with flat digital services revenue — mix, not top-line spend, is the variable to track in power-demand models.
insights.quote: reflecting faster short-term growth driven by compositional shifts from traditional web and data services toward more electricity intensive cloud, AI and data processing activity which will settle as the market matures
insights.locator: A logistic curve has been adopted to forecast the intensity

themes.theme: Australia as an APAC export hub for compute

insights.claim: An international demand component has been added to the model for the first time, on the thesis that Australia can act as an APAC data centre hub servicing workloads originating offshore.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: Australian data centre load is becoming an export-linked variable — domestic digitisation no longer caps the demand ceiling.
insights.locator: An international demand component is introduced

insights.claim: Benchmarking Australia's installed data centre capacity per unit of GDP against Asia Pacific excluding China and Australia implies roughly 5% to 10% of current Australian capacity already serves international demand, equal to about 1% to 1.5% of APAC consumption ex-China and ex-Australia.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: A small base with a large addressable pool — if Australia's share of APAC workloads doubles from ~1%, it materially moves the national load forecast.
insights.quote: These estimates suggest that around 5% to 10% of current capacity could be servicing international demand, equivalent to around 1% to 1.5% of APAC consumption (excluding China and Australia).
insights.locator: An international demand component is introduced

insights.claim: Public data on international data centre workloads is described as extremely limited, forcing the international demand estimate to rest on a capacity-to-GDP ratio comparison rather than observed flows.
insights.speaker: Shaista Shaista
insights.so_what: The most strategically important driver — export compute demand — is the least observable, so treat the international upside in Accelerated Transition as an assumption, not a measurement.
insights.quote: Public data on international workloads is extremely limited.
insights.locator: An international demand component is introduced
